# Week 4

## 1 Movie budgets and profits

There is another argument going on in the movie studio. Bob claims that production budgets are getting out of hand, and that the studio should focus on making cheaper movies. Chantal disagrees. She tells Bob that "Every dollar we spend on movie production is more than offset by the increase in movie profits".

### Step a

Set up a regression model to test Chantal's claim, and estimate it. That is, estimate:

\[Profits_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Budget_i + \varepsilon_i.\]

Print a summary of your estimated model. [2 points]

```{r}
# load data
movies <- read.delim("movies5.tsv")
movies$profit <- movies$revenue - movies$budget
# fit the model
m1 <- lm(profit ~ budget, data = movies)
summary(m1)
```

**Your Answer:**

We have estimated a linear regression to see how budget is related to profit, profit is the dependent variable and budget is the independent variable. they are both measured in dollars. The model estimates: predicted profit = -3,307,162.73 + 1.8301 x budget. The model uses all 909 movies that were given in the dataset. 

\newpage

### Step b

What is the estimated value of $\beta_1$ and how do you interpret it? [2 points]

**Your Answer:**

The estimated coefficient is 1.8301, as we calculated in step a. A one-dollar higher budget means the predicted profit is 1.83 dollars higher on average. This relationship doesn't prove that spending an extra dollar will cause profit to increase by this amount.

### Step c

Test for the null hypothesis that $\beta_1 \geq 0$. Report the p-value and state your conclusion. [2 points]

```{r}
# get the t-value
model_results <- summary(m1)
coefficient_table <- model_results$coefficients
t_value <- coefficient_table["budget", "t value"]
# find the p-value
degrees_freedom <- df.residual(m1)
p_value <- pt(t_value, df = degrees_freedom)
p_value
```

**Your Answer:**

The null hypothesis is H0: beta_1 >= 0, and the alternative hypothesis is H1: beta_1 < 0. In this case we use a 5% significance level. The t-value is approximately 20.80, and the one-sided p-value is approximately 1. the p-value is around 1, which is much greater then 0.05, so we can not reject the null hypothesis.. There is no evidence to be found of a negative relationship between profit and budget This test does not establish that beta_1 is greater than 1, only if its below 0. 

\newpage

### Step d

Next, estimate the model:

\[\log(Profits_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log(Budget_i) + \varepsilon_i.\]

When creating the variables Log Profits and Log Budget, make sure that movies with a Revenue or Budget of zero are assigned the value "NA". Print a summary of your estimated model. [2 points]

```{r}
# make log values
movies$log_profit <- NA
movies$log_budget <- NA
valid_budget <- movies$budget > 0 & movies$revenue > 0
movies$log_budget[valid_budget] <- log(movies$budget[valid_budget])
# keep positive profit
valid_profit <- valid_budget & movies$profit > 0
movies$log_profit[valid_profit] <- log(movies$profit[valid_profit])
m2 <- lm(log_profit ~ log_budget, data = movies)
summary(m2)
```

**Your Answer:**

We used log() in R to calculate the natural logarithms of profit as well as the budget. When revenue or budge is zero, we set both log values to NA, so they don't intervere with the calculations. We also set log profit to NA when profit is zero or negative, because we cannot calculate a usable logarithm for such values (Na). 

The estimated model is:

Predicted log profit = 7.64769 + 0.58680 × log budget.

R leaves out movies with missing log values, so the model uses 463 movies (out of the total 909 movies) The R-squared is 0.271. This means the model explains about 27.1% of the differences in log profit between these movies with log values that can actually be calculated. 

### Step e

What is the estimated value of $\beta_1$ and how do you interpret it? [2 points]

**Your Answer:**

The estimated coefficient of log budget (beta_1) is 0.58680, we calculated this in step d. we used logs for both budged and profit, a 1% higher budget is associated with approximately 0.59% higher profits.  This relationship applies to the movies included in the model, where calculations were possible. Here we can find that it does not prove that increasing a movie's budget causes its profit to increase

\newpage

### Step f

Which model has better fit? The level-level model or the log-log model? Explain. [2 points]

```{r}
# compare model fit
summary(m1)$r.squared
summary(m2)$r.squared
```

**Your Answer:**

The first model explains about 32.3 percent of the variation in profit, And the second model explains about 27.1% of the variation in log) profit.

The first model has a higher R-squared , but this does not necessarily mean it fits better, because there are differences: One model uses profit, while the other uses log profit. The first model also uses 909 movies, compared with 463 in the second model. 
Because of these differences between the models, it is not possible to decide which model fits better just by comparing their R-squared values.


### Step g

Who do you think is correct? Bob or Chantal? What would you advise the movie studio to do? [2 points]

```{r}
# find the 95% interval
confint(m1, "budget")
```

**Your Answer:**

Our results support Chantal more than it does Bob. The level-level model shows that a one-dollar higher budget is associated with about/around 1.83 dollars higher predicted profit. The 95% confidence interval is from 1.66 to 2.00. This entire interval is above 1, which helps to supporrt the claim of chantal.  The log-log model does also shows a positive relationship, but it measures the changes in percentages instead of dollars as before. 

However, the models do not prove that spending more causes higher profit. Other different factors, such as genre and audience demand, may affect both the budget and the profit. We advise the movie studio to compare the expected costs and revenue of each movie before choosing what the budget shoudl be. It should not always choose cheaper movies or assume that every extra dollar will lead to more profit, because this is not guaranteed.  

\newpage

## 2 First actor gender and movie budgets

### Step a

Make a plot with a 95% confidence interval with the mean log of budget on the y-axis, and whether the first actor of the movie is male or female on the x-axis. What do you conclude? [2 points]

```{r}
# use positive budgets
movies$log_budget <- NA
positive_budget <- movies$budget > 0
movies$log_budget[positive_budget] <- log(movies$budget[positive_budget])
# compare the groups
groups <- c("female", "male")
mean_log_budget <- numeric(2)
lower_budget <- numeric(2)
upper_budget <- numeric(2)
for (i in 1:2) {
  group_budget <- movies$log_budget[
    movies$first_actor_gender == groups[i]]
  group_budget <- group_budget[!is.na(group_budget)]
  mean_log_budget[i] <- mean(group_budget)
  interval <- t.test(group_budget, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int
  lower_budget[i] <- interval[1]
  upper_budget[i] <- interval[2]
}
# draw the graph
plot(1:2, mean_log_budget,
     main = "Mean log budget by first actor gender",
     xlab = "First actor gender", ylab = "Mean log budget",
     xaxt = "n", xlim = c(0.5, 2.5),
     ylim = range(lower_budget, upper_budget),
     pch = 19, col = "blue")
axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = c("Female", "Male"))
arrows(1:2, lower_budget, 1:2, upper_budget,
       angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.08, col = "blue")
```

**Your Answer:**

Movies with a female first actor have an average log budget of 16.62. For movies with a male first actor, it is higher than the females; 16.92. The 95% confidence intervals are 16.38–16.86 for the female group, and 16.77–17.06 for the male group.

The male group has a much higher average log budget. The intervals do overlap, but we need a actual statistical test to check whether or not the difference is significant or not. 

extra; We include movies with a budget above zero and a recorded first actor gender . Revenue does not need to be above zero because this question only looks at budget and gender, and so revenue is not important here. 

\newpage

### Step b

Estimate the following simple OLS model:

\[\log(budget_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1(FirstActorMale)_i + \varepsilon_i.\]

Is the estimated coefficient for $\beta_1$ significantly different from zero? How do you interpret its estimate, and how does this relate to your conclusion in 2a? [2 points]

```{r}
# make male equal to 1
is_male <- movies$first_actor_gender == "male"
movies$first_actor_male <- as.numeric(is_male)
# compare budgets
m3 <- lm(log_budget ~ first_actor_male, data = movies)
summary(m3)
# change to percent
budget_ratio <- exp(0.2963)
percentage_difference <- (budget_ratio - 1) * 100
percentage_difference
```

**Your Answer:**

The coefficient is 0.2963. The p-value is 0.0457, that is below 0.05. We therefore reject the null hypothesis that beta_1 equals zero. The difference between the two groups is statistically significant at the level of 5%.  We used 704 movies in total, 178 with a female first actor and 526 with a male first actor.

The average log budget is 0.2963 higher for the male group. This means that the geometric mean budget is about 34.49% higher than for the female group. In step a we also saw a higher average log budget for the male group, so the results do agree. The confidence intervals actually overlap, but the test still shows a actual significant difference. We are not able to say that having a male first actor causes a higher budget.

### Step c

Now, have a close look at your data frame. Can you find any instances of male first actors who are wrongly labelled as being female, or vice versa? What would such mislabelling mean for the coefficient you estimated under 2b? [2 points]

```{r}
# check actor labels
morgan_movies <- movies[movies$first_actor == "Morgan Freeman", ]
morgan_labels <- morgan_movies[, c("first_actor", "first_actor_gender")]
unique(morgan_labels)
jackie_movies <- movies[movies$first_actor == "Jackie Chan", ]
jackie_labels <- jackie_movies[, c("first_actor", "first_actor_gender")]
unique(jackie_labels)
```

**Your Answer:**

Morgan Freeman and Jackie Chan are men, but they are labelled as women in the dataset. Their movies are put in the wrong group (male/female group), this can affect the coefficient from step b and make it misleading because wrongly labelled groups. If these mistakes are not related to budget within each actual gender group, they usually mak estimated difference smaller. Otherwise, the difference could become either smaller or become larger. We did use the original labels, so we should check them before trusting the results.

# Week 5

## Movie release month and revenue predictions

### Step a

Create a plot of the mean profits by month of release. Do you see any indication that month of release matters to the profits of the movie? [2 points]

```{r}
# find monthly averages
profits_by_month <- aggregate(profit ~ release_month,
                             data = movies, FUN = mean)
profits_by_month$profit_millions <- profits_by_month$profit / 1000000
# draw the graph
plot(profits_by_month$release_month,
     profits_by_month$profit_millions,
     type = "b",
     pch = 19,
     col = "blue",
     xaxt = "n",
     main = "Average movie profit by release month",
     xlab = "Release month",
     ylab = "Mean profit (millions)")
axis(1, at = 1:12, labels = month.abb, cex.axis = 0.8)
profits_by_month
```

**Your Answer:**

Mean profit differs between release months. June has the highest mean profit, at about 123.49 million, followed by November at 105.28 million. ANnd September has the lowest mean profit, which is about 16.98 million.

The pattern goes up and down rather than steadily incresing throughout the year. This suggests that release month may matter, but the plot alone does not prove this,. Movies released in different months may also differ in budget, genre and other characteristics, which can also effect the profit. 

\newpage

### Step b

Estimate an OLS model which has as dependent variable the log of profits of a movie, and as independent variables the log of budget, a dummy for whether the movie was released in English or not, and a linear term for the month of release. Show a summary of the resulting model and interpret each coefficient. [4 points]

```{r}
# make english equal to 1
is_english <- movies$original_language == "en"
movies$english <- as.numeric(is_english)
# keep complete rows
needed_variables <- movies[, c("log_profit", "log_budget",
                              "english", "release_month")]
complete_movies <- complete.cases(needed_variables)
model_data <- movies[complete_movies, ]
# fit the model
m5b <- lm(log_profit ~ log_budget + english + release_month,
          data = model_data)
summary(m5b)
```

**Your Answer:**

The model uses 463 movies with positive profit and budget. When explaining each coefficient, we keep the other variables the same.

The intercept is 6.9683. This is the predicted log profit for a non-nglish movie with a budget of one dollar,which was released in month zero. month zero does not exist, so this has no actual practical meaning.

The log budget coefficient is 0.5770. A 1% higher budget is linked to about 0.58% higher profit.

The English coefficient is 0.7214. English movies have a predicted log profit that is 0.7214 higher than non-English movies. Their geometric mean profit iss therefore about 105.72% higher. we calculate this percentage using 100 × (exp(coefficient) − 1), with the full, unrounded coefficient.,
The release month coefficient is 0.0211. A release one month later in the same year is linked to about 2.13% higher profit. The model assumes the same percentage increase for each additional month.

These results do show relationships between profits and other variables, but do not prove that changing budget, language or release month causes profit to change.

### Step c

Test for the hypothesis that the coefficient that belongs to month of release is zero. [2 points]

```{r}
# test the month effect
summary(m5b)$coefficients["release_month", ]
```

**Your Answer:**

The null hypothesis is: beta_month = 0, and the alternative hypothesis is H1: beta_month is not zero. The t-value is around 1.147 and the p-value is 0.2519. Since this is higher than 0.05, we do not reject H0. There is no statistically significant linear month trend in this model, and this does not rule out an non-linear pattern across months

\newpage

### Step d

Based on your plot in a, do you consider the choice that month of release enters the model linearly under b reasonable? Estimate a specification that allows for a more flexible curve. In this new specification, test for the null hypothesis that month of release does not impact profits. This might require testing multiple terms at once. [4 points]

```{r}
# make month groups
model_data$month_group <- factor(model_data$release_month)
# fit the model
m5d <- lm(log_profit ~ log_budget + english + month_group,
          data = model_data)
model_results <- summary(m5d)
model_results$coefficients
# compare both models
m5d_restricted <- lm(log_profit ~ log_budget + english,
                     data = model_data)
anova(m5d_restricted, m5d)
```

**Your Answer:**

A linear month effect does not describe the plot well because profit rises and falls across the year. So we treat month as a category. January is the reference month, and the other 11 months each have their own coefficient. This does allow a separate pattern for each month.
The null hypothesis is that all 11 month coefficients equal zero. The alternative is that at least one is not zero. The joint F-test gives F(11, 449) = 1.7127 and p = 0.0679. At the 5% significance level, we do not reject H0. There is not enough evidence that month categories improve the model beyond budget and language. Thiss does not prove that release month is unrelated to the profit.

\newpage

### Step e

One executive at the studio wants to time the release of the movie to a specific month of the year such that they can maximize revenue. Based on your model under d, what would you advise the movie studio regarding the timing of the release of the movie? [2 points]

```{r}
# compare all months
month_options <- data.frame(log_budget = mean(model_data$log_budget),
                            english = 1,
                            month_group = factor(1:12,
                              levels = levels(model_data$month_group)))
# predict log profit
predicted_log_profit <- predict(m5d, newdata = month_options)
month.name[which.max(predicted_log_profit)]
```

**Your Answer:**

June has the highest predicted log profit when budget and language are being held constant. However, the joint test in step d is not significant at 5%, so we are not able to confidently recommend June as the 'best' month. The pattern is also based = on only the movies with positive profits and budgets.

The model predicts log profit, not directly revenue. For a fixed budget, higher profit also means higher revenue, but this does not prove that moving a release to June will actuallyincrease revenue. We would consider June as one option while also looking at competition, audience demand and the type of movie. So when looking at maximalising profits, multiple variables should be taken into consideration. 

\newpage

### Step f

The movie studio that you work at is releasing a new movie in 2026. It will be an English-spoken Thriller movie with a budget of 40,000,0000.

Estimate a model that is able to predict the revenue of this movie. Give its predicted revenue and include a 99% prediction interval. [6 points]

```{r}
# use positive revenue and budget
revenue_data <- subset(movies, revenue > 0 & budget > 0)
revenue_data$log_revenue <- log(revenue_data$revenue)
revenue_data$thriller <- as.numeric(revenue_data$genre == "Thriller")
# fit the model
m5f <- lm(log_revenue ~ log_budget + english + thriller + release_year,
          data = revenue_data)
summary(m5f)
# add the new movie
new_movie <- data.frame(log_budget = log(40000000), english = 1,
                        thriller = 1, release_year = 2026)
# predict revenue
prediction_log <- predict(m5f, newdata = new_movie,
                           interval = "prediction", level = 0.99)
exp(prediction_log)
```

**Your Answer:**

We estimated log revenue using log budget, English language, Thriller genre and last of all release year. The model uses 629 movies with positive revenue and budget, including movies that did make a loss.

For the English-spoken Thriller released in 2026, After converting the prediction back to dollars the revenue prediction is approx. 100.78 million dollars. This is the model's predicted median revenue, rather than its average revenue. The 99% prediction interval for this individual movie is around 2.11 million to 4,809.18 million dollars. We did used a prediction interval, and not an confidence interval for the calculation of the average revenue.

The interval is very wide, so the prediction is quite uncertain. It relies on the regression assumptions, including approximately normal errors with an constant variance on the log scale. Our data covers from 1990 to 2016, so using the model for 2026 also assumes that the estimated relationship continues beyond the actual observed years of the model. So when using this model outside of the observed years bring uncertaincy.
